prerequisites: To enroll in this course, it is necessary to have passed or be enrolled in all courses from lower years than the year in which this course is placed.

learning_outcomes.text: CG3 Knowledge in basic and technological subjects that enables them to learn new methods and theories, and provides them with versatility to adapt to new situations.

CG4 Ability to solve problems with initiative, decision-making, creativity, critical reasoning, and the ability to communicate and transmit knowledge, skills, and abilities in the field of industrial engineering in the Mechanical specialty.
CE14 Knowledge and use of the principles of strength of materials.
Understand the differences between rigid body and elastic body.
Understand the states of stress and strain in a deformable solid and the relationship between them.
Apply the acquired knowledge to determine the maximum stress values at a point in a deformable solid.
Understand the basic principles governing Strength of Materials.
Understand the relationships between different loads and the stresses they cause.
Apply the acquired knowledge to the determination of loads.
Apply the acquired knowledge about stresses to their calculation in bar elements.
Understand the fundamentals of deformations of bar elements.
Apply the acquired knowledge to the dimensioning of bar elements.

syllabus_topics: Introduction to static concepts necessary for the study of Strength of Materials
Vector. Scalar product and vector product
Types of constraints. Moment of a force
Static equilibrium. Equations. Elements subjected to 2 or 3 forces
Distributed forces and centroids
Reduction of a force system to a force-couple system
Frames and machines. Trusses.
Moments and products of inertia
Cables
Basic concepts of elasticity and strength of materials
Stresses and strains. Elastic solid
Relationships between stresses and unit strains.
Principles of relative stiffness and superposition.
Elastic equilibrium. Loads. Shear and bending moment diagrams
Tension-compression
Normal stress in a mechanical prism.
Deformations due to tension.
Statically determined problems. Hyperstatic problems.
Uniaxial tension or compression produced by thermal variations or assembly defects
Buckling
Fundamentals of compression buckling
Bending and shear
Beams: definition and types. Forces applied to beams.
Shear force and bending moment.
Relationships between shear force, bending moment and load.
Shear force and bending moment diagrams.
Types of bending. Hypotheses and limitations.
Normal stresses in the general case of oblique bending and asymmetric sections
Particular case of bending in symmetric sections. Navier's Law
Concept of section modulus. Optimal sections
Analysis of deformations: rotations and deflections.
Moment-curvature relationship. Elastic curve equation.
Theorems for calculating deformations
Hyperstatic bending
Other efforts
Fundamentals of shear
Fundamentals of torsion
assessment_rules: The final grade is based on Laboratory practices (10%), Supervised work (10%), Development questions exam (40%), and Objective questions exam (40%). For the Laboratory practices, Development questions exam, and Objective questions exam components to count, a minimum of 45% must be achieved in the final exam; this minimum is reduced to 40% if the Supervised work is passed. A minimum of 40% is required in the Objective questions exam part; failure to meet this minimum results in global evaluation being the only path to pass in the extraordinary resit. Students opting for global evaluation will take a final exam (60% problems, 40% conceptual) worth 100% of the grade, requiring at least 45% in each part. Unethical conduct, such as copying or using unauthorized electronic devices, will result in a 0.0 grade for the course.
